doc.title: Dawoud Sabu Adeyola interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 30, 2025

title: Stan Getz at Keystone Korner with Ahmad Jamal
summary: Being in the right place; Stan Getz asked how he kept up with Jamal.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution

blocks.x: know? So we have people like this you know. Of course Monk, you know Monk is doing it only the way he could do it, you know he always had a hat on or a goofy something covering his head. You know he’s dancing around the to the music on the stage. Freedom of expression is what we learned from these guys, that you can — in this music you can be free as you want to be or as you need to be. You don’t have to conform because your music and your art and the gift, your God-given gift is enough to qualify you to make a statement that you think needs to be made. And so Mingus, even long before — I had no idea that one day I would be called his protégé or be associated with him or play in the band. His band? I mean if you told me that in high school I would have told you no way, you’re crazy man. You know? But this stuff happened to me, you know? And I’m just thankful — and a lot of my students ask, they say how did you do all that stuff? I said a lot of it is just being in the right place at the right time. You can’t plan it. That’s why hang time among musicians, as you know, hang time is just as important as playing time. You know? Sometimes you’ve got to be, you’ve got to just be there to be noticed. I was playing in San Francisco one time at the Keystone Korner with Ahmad again, and on the break Stan Getz comes up to me there. And he says, “Hey man,” — and what I love about musicians is that they always have camaraderie. They come up and they have no [inaudible]. So he comes up to me and he says, “Hey Sabu, I see you here.” And he said, “Hey man, let me ask you a question.” I say, “Yeah, what?” He said, “How do you keep up with that guy? He’s all over the place.” You know? And he knows that a lot of the stuff we’re doing is not rehearsed you know, it’s just intuitive. He says, “How do you do that?” I told him I said, “Stan I just learned how to listen well.” You know?
Who was he referring to? How do you keep up —
Stan Getz. He’s talking about Ahmad.

I was playing with Ahmad Jamal. Yeah. And of course in Keystone Korner in those days, that was the spot. The audience, just like the Vanguard and Sweet Basil’s and places in New York, the audience is mainly musicians you know. I mean not just — I mean you’ve got Stan Getz here and Joe Henderson’s over there, and Woody Shaw is in the building, Mulgrew Miller is over there. You know. And there’s just all these great musicians man, they’re looking at you like yeah what are you going to do. But like I say, being in certain places in certain venues will get you opportunities that you might not get if you just stayed home or you just went to your own gigs and then you don’t socialize with the musicians, you don’t hang out with them.
Thanks — I think that was my composition I was playing, “Oasis for Jalilah” where I took an extended solo in the front of it.
